name: Diaminopyrimidine oxide

lead: Diaminopyrimidine oxide is a minoxidil-related ingredient in some hair-growth and anti-hair-loss lotions and shampoos. People with thinning hair use it hoping for thicker-looking hair.

Patents, including Korean filings from 2007 and 2008, describe such compositions as enhancing hair root activity. A 2026 network meta-analysis of therapies beyond minoxidil was reviewed, and no randomized trial of this ingredient was found.

paras: It is used in leave-on lotions or shampoos as part of a regular thinning-hair routine, with results judged over months.
No safety data were found in the reviewed sources. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Diaminopyrimidine oxide is a minoxidil-related ingredient in hair lotions and shampoos for thinning hair. Patents describe it as boosting hair root activity for thicker-looking hair. It is known mainly from patents, and trials were not found.

lead: Diaminopyrimidine oxide is a minoxidil-related ingredient used in some hair-growth and anti-hair-loss lotions and shampoos. It shares the pyrimidine N-oxide core of minoxidil, which is chemically 2,6-diamino-4-(piperidin-1-yl)pyrimidine 1-oxide, and in cosmetic patents the related compound carries a pyrrolidine ring in place of minoxidil's piperidine.[1][2][3]

People use it in topical products with the aim of thicker, fuller-looking hair and reduced shedding, usually as a minoxidil-like option sold as a cosmetic. Korean patent filings from 2007 and 2008 describe compositions of pyrrolidinyl diaminopyrimidine oxide for hair growth and for preventing hair loss.[1][2]

A 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis of off-label and unregulated therapies for male androgenetic alopecia found topical minoxidil 5% ranked most effective and listed topical diaminopyrimidine oxide 1% among other effective therapies, alongside topical melatonin, procyanidin, saw palmetto, cetirizine and finasteride.[4] No standalone randomized trial of diaminopyrimidine oxide was identified in the other materials reviewed.

paras: Minoxidil is a pyrimidine derivative with an N-oxide and a piperidine ring on the pyrimidine core.[3] The cosmetic patents describe a pyrrolidinyl analogue, so named because a five-membered pyrrolidine ring replaces the piperidine.[1][2] Wikipedia's minoxidil article does not discuss this analogue, so its properties are known mainly from the patent literature and the 2026 review.[4][3]

A 2008 Korean patent describes a hair-loss prevention composition containing henna extract, copper peptide and pyrrolidinyl diaminopyrimidine oxide, stating that it is intended to promote growth by enhancing hair root activity and thickening hair.[2] These are patent claims, not trial results.

The 2008 patent abstract describes a mixture of 30 to 60 weight percent henna extract, 30 to 60 percent copper peptide and 10 to 40 percent pyrrolidinyl diaminopyrimidine oxide, intended to promote growth by enhancing hair root activity, prevent loss and add volume by increasing hair thickness.[2]

Minoxidil was developed by Upjohn, named in 1963, introduced as an oral blood-pressure drug around 1971, and approved by the FDA as a topical treatment for male-pattern baldness in 1988 as Rogaine, after hair growth was noticed as a side effect; the FDA moved it to over-the-counter status in 1996.[3] Its exact mechanism is not fully understood: it is converted by the enzyme SULT1A1 to minoxidil sulfate, which opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels.[3] Whether cosmetic analogues follow the same pathway is not established, and the patents describe growth promotion without specifying a mechanism.[2]

No standalone clinical trial of diaminopyrimidine oxide was found. The 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and ClinicalTrials.gov on 23 January 2026 and included 23 studies (15 off-label and 8 topical minoxidil) measuring mean 6-month change in total hair density; it ranked topical minoxidil 5% most effective and listed diaminopyrimidine oxide 1% among other effective topical therapies, concluding that off-label options show potential.[4]
A registered trial of a scalp lotion for sensitive scalp syndrome (NCT05630027, 100 participants, started 2019) is listed, but its registration does not state that it tested this compound.[5]

Diaminopyrimidine oxide appears as an ingredient in direct-to-consumer hair serums and lotions marketed as minoxidil-like alternatives, which fits the broader trend of cosmetic hair actives discussed in the dermatology literature.[4] Regulation of such cosmetic ingredients differs between regions, and cosmetic labelling does not permit drug-style claims.

timeline.event: Korean patent filed for cosmetic composition containing pyrrolidinyl diaminopyrimidine oxide.[1]
Korean patent describes a hair-loss composition with henna, copper peptide and pyrrolidinyl diaminopyrimidine oxide.[2]
A network meta-analysis lists topical diaminopyrimidine oxide 1% among off-label therapies with positive hair-density results.[4]
